name: Face enameling

lead: Face enameling was a heavy form of face painting used to give the skin a younger, whiter, smoother look. It filled wrinkles and hollows with paste, covered the face with a white base, added rouge to the cheeks, and sometimes painted fine blue lines to suggest veins under translucent skin.

It was associated with actresses and courtesans, and with older upper-class women, and a few notable figures such as Queen Alexandra were rumoured to use it. Some period writers doubted that it worked as described.

paras: Period accounts describe cleansing the skin, filling lines with paste, applying a white enamel base and rouge, and optionally painting veins. Commercial products carried names such as White Liquid Enamel. The look was described as fixed, because strong expressions could crack the layer.

Many enamels used lead salts, and period critics described them as white lead in a cream base. Lead, mercury and arsenic in painted-look cosmetics were reported to corrode skin and require reapplication; zinc oxide and bismuth salts were later used as safer whiteners.

angle.text: Enameling covered lines and uneven colour with an opaque white layer topped with rouge, giving the appearance of smooth, translucent skin while it lasted.

lead: Face enameling was a form of face painting popular in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries that aimed to give the skin a younger, whiter look.[1] The term probably simply meant paint and was later replaced by the word make-up.[1]

The approach was layered: cleanse, fill wrinkles and hollows with a soft paste, paint a white base, then add rouge, and for some practitioners thin blue lines suggested visible veins and translucent skin.[1] The result was a smooth, pale complexion that critics said gave a fixed expression, since emotion would crack the paint.[1]
It built on earlier white-lead cosmetics such as Venetian ceruse, whose lead carbonate base was prized by the European aristocracy for pale skin.[2]

paras: Period accounts describe an alkaline wash, a soft filler paste for hollows and lines, a white base and rouge.[1] A New York studio on Broadway offered enameling in 1869, with prices that rose with the length of the effect.[1]
Commercial enamels included Hunt's White Liquid Enamel (1864), Chastellar's (1866), Hunt's White French Skin Enamel (1885), Marie Earle's Émail 77 and Helena Rubinstein's Email du Visage.[1]

Chorus girls, courtesans and other women of ill repute were most associated with the practice, while some older upper-class women may have used it and middle-class women generally avoided it.[1] Queen Alexandra reportedly had her face enamelled near age 74, though the source treats this as conjecture; photographs of her were also retouched.[1]
In 1908 the writer Potter argued that enameling was impossible and that rumours about prominent women were gossip, based on recipes using bismuth or other metal salts.[1]

Many practitioners used lead salts, described by critics as white lead in a cream base, and commentators warned of clogged pores.[1] Painted-look enamels in the Victorian era reportedly contained lead, mercury and arsenic and corroded skin, so wearers reapplied to cover damage; belladonna eye drops used alongside could cause blindness with prolonged use.[3]

Lead cosmetics caused symptoms including abdominal pain, paralysis and convulsions in long-term use, according to accounts of Venetian ceruse.[2] A McMaster University study that re-created 16th-to-19th-century white lead recipes reported that most probably did not kill through skin absorption, though a vinegar-and-lead mixture passed the most lead through skin; the author calls the findings preliminary.[4]
By the late nineteenth century zinc oxide and bismuth salts were increasingly used as safer whiteners.[1]

No studies found. Laboratory work on historical recipes exists: the McMaster team found re-created white lead makeup looked subtle rather than mask-like, raising diffuse reflectance for a soft-focus, youthful look.[4]
